newsitem.title: USA: Intel sees better-than-expected third quarter.
newsitem.headline: Intel sees better-than-expected third quarter.

text.p: Microprocessor giant Intel Corp. Monday provided an unexpected boost to the technology sector, telling investors that revenues for the third quarter would be better than previously forecast.

In a statement issued after the market closed, Intel said revenues for the three months ended in September were expected to be about 5 percent higher than its second-quarter revenues of $4.62 billion, rather than flat with that quarter as it once expected.
The upbeat forecast sent Intel's stock soaring $3.375 to $92 in after-hours trading. Earlier, it ended at $88.625, up 50 cents, on Nasdaq.
Analysts predicted the positive outlook for Intel, which provides the microprocessors for about 80 percent of the personal computers sold in the world, would lift other technology stocks Tuesday.
"This indicates that the PC industry is doing quite well," said analyst Jon Joseph of Montgomery Securities.

"It's got to be very positive for the industry," said John Lazlo of brokerage PaineWebber. "First, it suggests PC demand is at least as robust as analysts have been forecasting -- somewhere in the mid-teens growth" for the year.

The Montgomery and PaineWebber analysts, as well as analysts at Robertson, Stephens & Co., all said they would increase their third-quarter earnings estimates for Intel as a result of the company's upbeat outlook.
According to First Call, Intel was expected to report a profit in the third quarter of $1.14 a share.

In last year's third quarter, Intel reported profits of $931 million or $1.05 per share, on sales of $4.17 billion. The quarter included a gain of $37 million before taxes, or 3 cents per share after taxes.
Intel plans to report results Oct. 14.
When Intel reported its second-quarter earnings in July, it said third-quarter revenues would be flat with the second quarter.

In its statement, Intel said gross margins -- the difference between the sales price for its products and the costs of raw materials and manufacturing -- would be better than its model of 50 percent, plus or minus a couple of points.
Intel's gross margin in the second quarter was 53 percent.

Intel said business levels were hard to predict because the semiconductor industry is in a so-called "turns" environment, in which manufacturers order chips just before they need them in the assembly line.
"Business levels are inherently difficult to predict and appear to be better than originally expected," it said in a statement.
Executives would not specify which products were selling better than previously expected.

But spokesman Tom Waldrop said that in general, "We see lifts from the conversion of the business-market basic PCs from Pentium to Pentium Pros," Intel's latest microprocessor, "And, in the home market, an exciting array of products hitting the home market,"
Montgomery's Joseph said it was rare for Intel to make such an announcement ahead of its formal earnings report.
"It hasn't happened in four years," he said.
